title: Jev classifies a tick's kind of work; config maps work to model
description:
Jev classifies the KIND OF WORK a tick is; the orchestrator's config maps a kind of work to a model.

THE SHAPE, and why it is this way round (operator, 2026-09-22). Jev is not asked which
model to use. It is asked what the work IS - a closed enum of work types - and the config
decides what that is worth. Each decision sits with whoever can make it: the classifier
judges the tick, the operator's table judges the cost.

That separation buys four things:
  - Changing model policy does not invalidate a recorded classification. Swap the model
    lineup, add a tier, change your mind about budget: you edit a table. "This is a docs
    tick" stays true; "this deserves flash" was only ever true against one lineup.
  - The recorded evidence means something to a person reading the run later. A work type
    explains why a run went the way it did; a tier name does not.
  - It matches the config shape that already exists. [roles.*.tiers.<name>] already maps a
    name to a model overlay; a work type is another key into that kind of table.
  - It is a better task for Jev. A closed enum is its sweet spot; weighing cost against
    capability is policy, not classification.

It also dissolves the promotion question below. "Nothing starts high on a DESCRIPTION"
guarded against prose buying an expensive model. A classified work type is not prose - it
is a fact, and the table decides what it costs - so promotion stops being a special case.

WHY, and what it changes. Today a first attempt's tier comes from [[tier_policy.start]] rules matching STRUCTURAL FACTS - type, role, priority, wave, how many ticks it blocks. Those are proxies for complexity, not judgements of it, and `max_blocks = 0` ("the mark of a mechanical tick") is about as close as a fact gets. A deterministic orchestrator cannot read a tick and decide whether the work is hard.

Operator, 2026-09-22: it should be able to ask. Jev (TypeSafe AI, early access 15 Sept 2026) is a "System One" model - text in, TYPED probabilistic decisions out, with confidence, in one parallel pass. About $0.042 per million input tokens with free output, 40-200x faster than a frontier model.

Three properties that make it the right instrument rather than just a cheap one:
  - It cannot produce a type error. The tier vocabulary is a closed enum (isKnownTier refuses anything else); a text model can answer "medium-high" and needs validating, Jev structurally cannot.
  - It returns CONFIDENCE. Low confidence is a third answer, not a coin flip - fall back to the policy's default, the same way run.cost_source distinguishes a zero from an unknown.
  - The cost is a rounding error, so "do not pay a model to decide what to pay a model" stops being an objection.

THE DECISION THAT OVERRIDES AN EXISTING RULE, stated so nobody later reads it as a bug.

internal/runconfig/tierpolicy.go says, and load.go enforces:

    "The one rule that makes the ladder a ladder rather than a wish: facts may
     make a first attempt CHEAPER, never dearer."
    "nothing starts high on a description - expense is earned by a failed
     attempt, not asserted by a rule"

Operator, 2026-09-22: "i think it should be allowed to go dearer."

That rule exists to stop a DESCRIPTION buying an expensive model - an author, or a model reading prose, talking its way up the ladder. The reason it is being relaxed is that Jev is not a description: it is a classifier with a confidence score, on a closed enum, priced so low that a wrong cheap guess costs more in wasted attempts than every classification in the epic costs to make. Starting a genuinely complex tick on flash so it can fail and climb is the waste the operator objected to, and it is real: a failed attempt is a model's full run, a wall clock, and a gate.

So promotion is allowed, BOUNDED BY THE CEILING. What is NOT relaxed:
  - The ceiling still bounds everything. At the ceiling the next actor is a person, not a bigger model.
  - Failure still escalates underneath. Jev picks a START; a failed attempt still earns a rung.
  - A tick's own prose still cannot promote it. The classifier may, an assertion in a description may not.

SHAPE
  0. A tick CARRYING A ROLE IS NEVER CLASSIFIED. [roles.*] already maps review and
     closeout to a model; asking Jev as well produces a worse answer from a menu that
     has no right option on it, as the measurement below found. The classifier is for
     implementation ticks. This is a precondition, not a fallback.
  1. First dispatch of a role-less tick: the orchestrator asks Jev which WORK TYPE the
     tick is, from a closed enum declared in config, plus the full probability
     distribution. It is never asked for a model or a tier.
  2. The answer is written to the run branch as a decision record, like the review and closeout exchanges already are - "so a restart re-reads them instead of re-asking a model it already paid". This is axiom 1, not thrift: a re-derivation must reach the same dispatch, and a recorded classification does while a re-ask only probably does.
  3. Later passes, including after a restart, READ the record. Jev is asked once per tick.
  4. ROUTING IS ON PROBABILITY MASS, NOT ON THE ARGMAX PLUS A CONFIDENCE THRESHOLD.
     The dear model is chosen when the mass on the dear work types clears a threshold
     - with today's lineup, when P(design) + P(diagnosis) > 0.50. A tick split 0.45
     design / 0.42 construction is not an unknown to be defaulted; it is a tick with
     0.45 of design in it, and the mass rule spends that instead of discarding it.
     One tunable (the mass threshold) replaces two (argmax plus a confidence floor).
     No answer at all, or Jev unavailable: fall back to [[tier_policy.start]] and the
     default. The feature degrades to today's behaviour rather than stopping a run.
  5. The config maps work type -> model, beside the existing [roles.*.tiers.*] overlays.
     A work type with no mapping falls back to the default, and says so, rather than
     failing a dispatch on a table someone forgot to extend.
  6. The recorded work type is an input to the policy, not a replacement for it: the
     ceiling, the step and the failure ladder all still apply on top.

OPEN, and worth settling before building:
  - Jev is in LIMITED EARLY ACCESS. Confirm access and terms before this becomes load-bearing, and keep (4) so the factory works without it.
  - What exactly is Jev shown? The tick's title, description and acceptance criteria are the obvious input; whether it also sees the repository's own conventions is a real question, because a tick that is trivial in one codebase is not in another.
  - The MASS THRESHOLD is 0.50 provisionally, which routes 29% of a 49-tick sample to
     the dear model. What is NOT settled is whether 29% is the right fraction, and that
     sample cannot say: every tick in it ran at its role's base model with no
     [tier_policy] declared, and its retries were wall-clock and hold failures rather
     than capability failures. Settle it by running an epic with the policy ON.
  - The work-type enum is PROPOSED BELOW and no longer open. What remains open about it
     is whether `construction` sits on the right side of the flash/full line, which the
     measurement below is the way to settle.
  - Two models today (GLM 5.3 Flash, GLM 5.3), so several work types will map to the same
     model. That is fine and is the point: the enum describes the work, the table describes
     what it costs, and they are allowed to be different shapes.

THE WORK-TYPE ENUM (operator asked for a proposal, 2026-09-22; this is it)

The axis is INFERENCE UNDER UNCERTAINTY - how much of the work is deciding what to do
rather than doing it. Size and risk were considered and rejected: a large mechanical edit
is still mechanical, and a risky one-line change is still one line. What separated flash
from full in this week's actual runs was how much had to be worked out.

  mechanical    the change is stated, not decided. Done is knowable by construction.
  translation   a known pattern applied to new material. Done is knowable by comparison.
  construction  build to a stated spec; decisions are local. Done is the acceptance.
  diagnosis     cause unknown. Form and discard hypotheses against evidence. Done is
                knowable only once the cause is found.
  design        the shape itself is in question, and the tick's own framing may be wrong.
                Done is knowable only by argument.

Ordered on purpose. Adding a third model later moves ONE boundary instead of
re-classifying anything, and the recorded classifications stay valid.

GROUNDED IN TICKS THIS REPOSITORY ACTUALLY RAN, which is the test of whether an enum is
real rather than plausible:

  mechanical    f8l - delete hello.txt and goodbye.txt. GLM did it in nine tool calls.
  translation   lk9 - add a guard test in the shape of the existing `serial:` guard.
  construction  8xd - a streaming tar reader to a stated spec.
                prs - put the ticfac binaries in the orchestrator image.
  diagnosis     qsn - a detached `git maintenance` child corrupting the NEXT test's
                fixture; found with GIT_TRACE2_EVENT after two wrong hypotheses.
                m78 - the tracker and the gate both naming their worktree `tree`.
  design        yoh - where the orchestrator runs.
                wne - this ticket.

MAPPING, with two models today:

    mechanical, translation, construction  -> glm-5.3-flash
    diagnosis, design                      -> glm-5.3

`construction` is deliberately the contentious one. It is the boundary case, and it is
where the failure ladder earns its keep rather than where classification has to be right.

WHY THIS IS NOT ticks' `type` FIELD. `task`/`bug`/`epic` describes the TICKET - who filed
it and what it is about. This describes the WORK. A bug can be mechanical (a typo with a
known fix) or diagnosis (an intermittent failure with no repro), and those two want
different models. Keeping them separate is the whole point.

JEV IS FALLIBLE, AND THE LADDER ALREADY HANDLES IT (operator, 2026-09-22: "a tick that
fails on a low model may need to get mechanically upgraded to a larger").

That is the existing mechanism, unchanged: Jev picks the START, each FAILED attempt earns
a rung upward, bounded by the ceiling, and at the ceiling the next actor is a person.
A mis-classified `construction` tick fails on flash and becomes full with nobody in the
loop. Classification makes the FIRST attempt smarter; escalation makes a wrong
classification cheap. Neither has to be perfect for the pair to be good.

MEASURED, 2026-09-22, BEFORE BUILDING ANY OF IT. 49 closed ticks from epics 9pd/dha/ncv,
three Jev calls, $0.0022. The full result is the note on this tick; the three things it
changed in the spec above are (0) role-carrying ticks are never classified, (4) routing
is on probability mass, and the mass threshold replacing the confidence threshold in
OPEN. What it could NOT settle is the flash/full boundary itself, for the reason stated
there - so the boundary stays provisional until an epic runs with the policy on.

Worth keeping in view: the sample classified only 2 of 49 as `diagnosis`, and the criteria
were right to. A defect is filed AFTER its cause is found, so the tick text names the fix.
The diagnosis happens in the session that writes the tick, not in the tick. Any future
measurement of that category needs ticks filed from a symptom.
notes:
2026-09-22 14:47 - WHERE THE MAPPING LIVES (operator, 2026-09-22): 'the mapping is a config for the factory'.

So the split is:

  REPO, .tick/runners.toml    what the work IS - the work-type enum, the escalation
                              policy, the ceiling. Facts about this project's work.
  FACTORY, deployment config  what a work type COSTS - which model serves it. Facts about
                              this deployment's gateway, account and spend.

That is consistent with where the factory already keeps this kind of fact: wrangler.toml
binds SWEEP_MAX_TIER = 'economy', so tier vocabulary is ALREADY partly deployment-level,
beside RUN_MAX_COST_USD, FACTORY_MAX_INSTANCES and the gateway credentials.

It also gives the right failure direction: a repo cannot name a model the factory does not
serve, because the factory owns the gateway. A repo asking for something unavailable is
refused or falls back, rather than a run dying at the first dispatch on a credential the
project was never going to have.

ONE CONFLICT TO SETTLE BEFORE BUILDING, flagged rather than left to be discovered:
[roles.*.tiers.<name>] in runners.toml TODAY holds per-repo model overlays. profiles-herdr/
pins cloudflare-workers-ai/@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 per role. If the work-type -> model mapping
becomes factory config, those overlap. Three defensible answers:

  a) Factory wins outright; repo overlays become advisory or are removed. Simplest, and
     matches 'the factory owns the models'. Costs a repo the ability to say 'this project
     needs the bigger model for translation work'.
  b) Repo may override WITHIN what the factory serves. More expressive; needs the factory
     to publish its available models so a repo's choice can be validated rather than
     discovered at dispatch.
  c) Repo declares work types only, factory declares everything about models, and the
     per-role overlays are deleted. Cleanest conceptually, biggest change to what exists.

I would take (b) if repos genuinely differ in what they need, and (a) if they do not -
which is an empirical question about the enrolled repositories, not a taste question.
2026-09-22 14:50 - THE JEV CALL, concretely (docs.typesafe.ai, read 2026-09-22).

Jev has three primitives - Choice (select from options), Score (rubric-based), Noul (truth
statements). This is a Choice. The schema:

    {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "What kind of work is this tick?",
      "criteria": {
        "mechanical":   {"what": "...", "not_for": "...", "examples": [...]},
        "translation":  {...},
        "construction": {...},
        "diagnosis":    {...},
        "design":       {...}
      }
    }

ANSWERING 'can each type carry a deeper description' (operator): yes. A criteria value may
be a plain string, null when the name speaks for itself, or an OBJECT with custom fields -
the docs give 'what', 'not_for', 'examples'. Up to 255 options, so five is nothing.

'not_for' is the field that earns its place here. construction-vs-diagnosis is the
contentious boundary in the enum above, and a negative example pins a boundary better than
another positive one. Write the criteria with the boundary cases from this repository:
8xd (construction: the shape was stated, the work was building it) against qsn (diagnosis:
the cause was unknown and two hypotheses were wrong first).

The response carries the FULL PROBABILITY MAP, not just a winner:

    {"choice": "construction", "confidence": 0.85,
     "probabilities": {"construction": 0.85, "diagnosis": 0.10, ...}}

Confidence is computed from the shape of that distribution. So a tick at 0.45/0.40 between
construction and diagnosis is VISIBLY marginal rather than silently decided - record the
distribution, not just the choice, and the 'low confidence falls back to policy' rule has
something honest to read.

ONE CALL PER EPIC (operator, 2026-09-22: 'jev can handle arrays, so maybe it can classify
entire epic in one go'). The docs: 'All three question types can be mixed in a single API
call. Every question is evaluated in parallel and in isolation against the same state in
one go.' So: state = the epic's ticks, one Choice per tick, one round trip.

'In isolation' is the property that makes this safe rather than merely cheap: tick A's
classification cannot drag tick B's.

BUT NOT ONCE AT THE START. Ticks appear mid-run - planning fleshes out the next epic,
close-out adds ticks, findings get filed as ticks during a run. So the rule is CLASSIFY THE
UNCLASSIFIED on each pass: usually a no-op, occasionally a small batch, never a re-ask for
a tick already recorded. That also keeps it consistent with D33, where every pass
re-derives the world from durable authorities - the classification record IS the durable
authority here.
2026-09-22 15:08 - WORK-TYPE CLASSIFICATION: FIRST MEASUREMENT (tick wne, 2026-09-22)

49 closed ticks from epics 9pd/dha/ncv, classified by Jev in 3 calls (one per epic,
one Choice question per tick against shared state). 52,945 input tokens, $0.0022.

  construction 17   design 15   mechanical 8   translation 7   diagnosis 2
  confidence: median 0.66, 13 of 49 below 0.50

WHAT HELD UP
  The high-confidence end is right. cxk/e08 "port X to the Workflow host" -> translation
  at 0.95/0.92. 19l, 54n, 9fc, b50 -> design at 0.98+, and those genuinely are ticks
  where the framing was in question. emk, pbb, ef7, 7zs -> construction at ~0.90.
  Above about 0.75 the labels are ones a person who ran this work would also pick.

THREE DEFECTS IN THE CRITERIA, in order of how much they cost

1. PROCESS TICKS MUST NOT BE CLASSIFIED AT ALL.
   Three ticks in the set carry a --role. Same kind of work, three different answers:
     h0f  role=review    -> mechanical 0.32
     pxc  role=review    -> diagnosis   0.61
     3q0  role=closeout  -> design      0.99
   The enum has no category for "read a diff and judge it", so Jev picks from five
   wrong options. It also does not need one: [roles.*] already maps role -> model.
   Fix: skip any tick with a role. The classifier is for implementation ticks.

2. THE COST-CRITICAL BOUNDARY IS THE ONE JEV IS LEAST SURE OF.
   Every low-confidence case is construction-vs-design or mechanical-vs-diagnosis -
   that is, exactly the flash/full line, never a cheap-vs-cheap confusion:
     sz0 design 0.41 / construction 0.34    n4h design 0.45 / construction 0.42
     cwa design 0.45 / construction 0.18    0dc mechanical 0.35 / diagnosis 0.33
   This is not a failure of the run; it is the shape of the problem, and it means the
   routing rule matters as much as the criteria do (see below).

3. THE DATASET UNDER-REPRESENTS DIAGNOSIS, AND THAT IS THE DATASET'S FAULT.
   Only 2 of 49 classified diagnosis, and one of those is a review tick. But the
   criteria are behaving correctly: a defect is filed AFTER its cause is found, so
   the tick text names the fix. "Adoption picks the FIRST attempt, not the latest"
   reads mechanical because by the time it was written, it was. Real diagnosis work
   happens in the session that files the tick, not in the tick. A future set needs
   ticks filed from a symptom, not from a diagnosis.

ROUTING RULE: USE THE PROBABILITY MASS, NOT THE ARGMAX
   argmax alone                        -> 17/49 (35%) on full
   argmax, low confidence falls back   -> 26/49 (53%) on full   <- the blunt version
   P(design)+P(diagnosis) > 0.50       -> 14/49 (29%) on full

   The mass rule is better for the reason the confidence fallback is worse: a tick
   split 0.45/0.42 between design and construction is not an unknown to be defaulted,
   it is a tick with 0.45 of design in it. The mass rule spends the confidence
   instead of discarding it, and it removes the confidence threshold as a tunable -
   one number (the mass threshold) instead of two.

   Not yet validated: whether 29% is the RIGHT fraction. This set cannot say, because
   every tick ran at its role's base model with no [tier_policy], and the retries in
   it were wall-clock and hold failures, not capability failures. The boundary can
   only be measured by running an epic with the policy on.
acceptance_criteria: A dispatch chooses its worker model from a Jev-classified work type recorded on the run branch: a role-carrying tick is never classified, a role-less tick is classified once and re-read on every later pass including after a restart, routing is on probability mass over the dear work types, an absent or unreachable classifier degrades to [[tier_policy.start]] rather than stopping a run, and the ceiling and the failure ladder still bound everything on top. Proven by a cold re-derivation reaching the same dispatch as the warm process.
